Koz
kŏz
n. (head of a priestly house whose register could not be found)
Hebrew Qots, meaning a thorn. The house of Koz held the seventh priestly course under David; at the return from Babylon its descendants could not produce their genealogy and were put from the priesthood.

Biblical Definition

Among the returning exiles were men who claimed priestly descent and could not prove it: “And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai; which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name” (Ezra 2:61). The result was immediate and severe: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). Nehemiah records the identical ruling in his own list: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Nehemiah 7:64). Yet the name is not left under a cloud. When the wall was rebuilt, a grandson of Koz is found working on it and working twice: “And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz” (Nehemiah 3:4). He appears again a few verses on, repairing another piece from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of it. Barred from the altar or not, the house of Koz was on the wall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Koz; the name belongs to a priestly family of Judah, the seventh of the courses appointed by David.

KOZ, n. The head of a priestly house; in Hebrew, a thorn.

REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings; a book of record.

GENEALOGY, n. An account of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in order.

POLLUTED, pp. Defiled; made unclean or impure; rendered unfit for sacred use.

COURSE, n. The order of succession in which the priests served at the temple, by divisions.

Key Scripture

Ezra 2:61 — "And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai; which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name:"

Ezra 2:62 — "These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."

Nehemiah 7:64 — "These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."

Nehemiah 3:4 — "And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana."

Modern Corruption

The exclusion is read as bureaucratic cruelty, and the positive lesson — that a man barred from one office found another and laboured in it — is never drawn.

expand to see more

The ruling looks harsh to modern eyes: men who believed themselves priests were put out because a document was missing. But the priesthood was hereditary by divine appointment, not by conviction or self-assessment, and a man who could not show his descent could not stand between Israel and God on the assumption that he probably qualified. Ezra's governor added a mercy the objection usually omits: they were not to eat of the most holy things until there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim — the case was suspended, not closed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering is what the house of Koz did next. Barred from the altar, Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz shows up in Nehemiah's wall-building register repairing one section, and then a second section. He is one of very few men in that chapter credited with two pieces of work. A family excluded from the office it wanted did not withdraw; it picked up trowels. The New Testament's answer to the whole anxiety is that in Christ every believer's register is secure, for He is the High Priest whose genealogy and whose office are both beyond question.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Qots (H6976), a thorn; yachas (H3187), to reckon by genealogy; gaal (H1351), to defile or pollute; kehunnah (H3550), the priesthood.

Hebrew Qots (H6976) — Koz, a thorn; head of the seventh priestly course.

Hebrew yachas (H3187) — to reckon genealogically; reckoned by genealogy.

Hebrew gaal (H1351) — to defile, pollute; as polluted, put from the priesthood.

Hebrew kethab / sepher (H5612) — the register they sought and did not find.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, repair; Meremoth repaired, Nehemiah 3:4.

Usage

"“The children of Koz” — among those who could not prove their descent."

"“As polluted, put from the priesthood” — the ruling given twice."

"“Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz” — the same house, on the wall."
